text.p: LONDON - Norway's Kvaerner ASA has worked fast to integrate the Trafalgar House engineering and construction units it bought this spring but chief executive Erik Toenseth said on Tuesday he felt no pressure to sell off its non-core units.

Speaking from Trafalgar House's old London headquarters, overlooking central London's Piccadilly, Toenseth said he understood the anxiety of some investors that Kvaerner had inherited problems as well as assets by buying Trafalgar.
"We're unhappy that people are unhappy," he told Reuters.
He gave little away about how the firm intends to divest Cunard, the cruise shipping line that came in the Trafalgar House package, which Kvaerner says it does not want to keep.
"Long-term, we are unlikely to be the sole shareholder in Cunard... we would be happy to be investors on a small or large scale," he said, declining to elaborate on any timeframe.

He said, however, that progress in integrating Trafalgar's three core units -- in construction, metals and process engineering -- with Kvaerner's existing offshore and pulping engineering businesses had been swift and reassuring.
"The core business of Trafalgar House is the kind of business we are used to and therefore it's been fairly quick to get a feel for where we are," Toenseth said.
"I think a lot will be achieved fairly soon, and then it will take longer to fine-tune it," he added.

Each of the six areas now forming the core of Kvaerner's business -- shipbuilding, process engineering, oil and gas engineering, construction, metals and pulping -- has been exposed to sharp cyclical downturns in recent years.

Toenseth said his goal was a closely-integrated global Kvaerner group that can share and shift around core competencies among different business areas to prevent shocks of the type that dogged Trafalgar House units, in particular, in the past.

Asked how much time he needed he said, "I think organisation is a continuous process, so there will not be any end. But it will probably take a couple of years before we can say that now we have basically sorted out all the historic challenges'."
Shipbuilding, inhenerently more complex, would take longer.
Norway's share market took fright earlier this month when Kvaerner's half-year results showed a sharp fall in both pretax profit (down 56 percent) and operating profit (off 60 percent).

Although the company said most of the blame lay with deeper-than-expected losses at its pulping engineering unit, mainly in the U.S., which have now eased, Kvaerner's shares have been unable to recover their heights seen earlier in 1996.
Toenseth said change throughout the group had been swift.
He said he had been surprised at the pent-up energy Kvaerner found within the Trafalgar engineering and construction units, and which he saw "suddenly released in the new situation."
In the past, companies inside Trafalgar House had suffered from its financial insecurity and intra-group strains, Toenseth added, in a frank critique of the conglomerate.

"As long as (staff) were in the situation where they didn't really know what the future would involve, they wouldn't approach markets -- or technology, or partners -- in an aggressive and positive way. That has changed," he said.
"We want to help make them more outward, more ambitious, more fighting for new projects and knowing that they are long-term winners. We try to give them that self-confidence."
From September, Toenseth intends all six business unit managers, along with finance chief Jan Heggelund, to join him in a new corporate headquarters in St James, near Piccadilly.
The eight men will share an office, he says, and so seek to maintain in the new structure a closeness and open communication style that Toenseth claims he established at Kvaerner in Norway.

It should, he stressed, feel like a much smaller organisation than before for the former Trafalgar employees -- despite the fact that they have joined Norway's second largest listed company and now have nearly 60,000 colleagues.
